transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-11-12
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Ruiz (Redwood SE), Lena Cho (Aurora CTO), Marcus Voss (Head of ML), Priya Singh (SRE)

Summary (auto): POC will run a 2-week benchmark comparing Redwood hosted vs Dedicated for Aurora's chat summarization workload. Success criteria: 95th latency < 500ms for short responses, average cost per 1k output tokens under $0.80 (goal), accuracy/quality within 3% of current baseline. Action items captured.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Maya, account lead at Redwood. daniel is our systems engineer.
[00:07] Daniel: hi all, run the perf side, happy to scope benchmarks.
[00:10] Lena: hi, thanks. Lena here, CTO at Aurora. Marcus and Priya are on. we've been evaluating inference options for our live chat summarization product.
[00:18] Marcus: main thing for us is unit economics and tail latency. we run about 250 QPS peak across shards, often 4k token input max for some flows but most are 200-500 tokens.
[00:29] Priya: also need to ensure any Private/VPC deployment can talk to our KMS and respect egress policies. SOC2 is required.
[00:36] Maya: great, that aligns with what we usually see. quick agenda: workload sizing, success criteria, cost modeling (per-token estimates + batching/caching knobs), and then benchmark plan and timeline. sound ok?
[00:45] Lena: yep.
[00:46] Daniel: before we get into cost numbers, can you walk through your QPS distribution, avg input/out tokens per request?
[00:52] Marcus: sure. 250 peak QPS but effective concurrent model requests ~40 across workers; bursts up to 400 for short windows. average input length ~350 tokens, average generated output ~120 tokens. heavy tail: 5% of requests hit >2k output tokens.
[01:10] Daniel: ok that distribution is helpful. for cost modeling we typically separate request-level costs: model inference per token + overheads like routing, KV cache misses, and session state. our per-token estimates vary by model and deployment. for a quantized 7B variant on dedicated infra we might see $0.0006 per output token equivalent, hosted higher due to multi-tenant overhead.
[01:30] Lena: can you unpack that - what do you mean by quantized and per-token equivalent?
[01:33] Daniel: sure. quantized means we use int8/int4 kernels to reduce GPU memory and improve throughput. per-token equivalent normalizes cost across variants — it factors in batching efficiency, prefix caching savings, and amortized GPU occupancy. so a small model with aggressive batching might have lower per-token cost but worse latency.
[01:50] Marcus: what's our latency SLO? we need 95th < 500ms for short responses and p95 < 1s for longer flows.
[01:58] Daniel: targetable. with Dedicated you can get tighter tails because you avoid noisy neighbors and can tune batch sizes and accumulated latency windows. we also have KV/prefix caching that helps for repeated session prompts. cache hit ratios dramatically change cost.
[02:11] Maya: quick note on hosted vs dedicated pricing: hosted is simple per-token + request fees; dedicated is a committed monthly/annual SKU with reserved GPU pools — higher fixed cost but lower marginal token price. we'll send a spreadsheet with both scenarios.
[02:23] Lena: what's a realistic ballpark per 1k tokens for hosted vs dedicated for our workload?
[02:28] Daniel: ballpark (very rough): hosted with a mid-size open model ~ $1.20 per 1k output tokens given your mixed input lengths; dedicated quantized path could bring that down to ~$0.45–0.75 per 1k depending on batch strategy and cache hit rates. if you use a larger model for quality we'd be in the $1.00–1.80 range hosted, $0.70–1.20 dedicated.
[02:48] Marcus: those ranges help. what's the impact of batching? we worry about latency when you accumulate batches.
[02:53] Daniel: batching increases throughput and lowers per-token cost by improving GPU fill, but it adds a batching latency term. we can configure dynamic batching windows: e.g., target 5–10ms accumulation for low latency SLOs vs 50–100ms for cost-optimized. For your 95th < 500ms target, we recommend strict batching windows and more dedicated capacity.
[03:12] Priya: how does prefix/KV cache factor in? many of our sessions repeat similar system prompts.
[03:16] Daniel: prefix/KV cache stores previous key/value states for repeated prefixes — big win if you have lots of conversational state reuse. a 70% cache hit could cut token compute by similar fraction for the repeated prefix portion. however, cache hits add memory pressure and complexity in multi-tenant hosted setups; dedicated gives you more predictable cache sizing.
[03:33] Lena: security is big: we need VPC connection, SAML/SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration. can Dedicated or Private cover that?
[03:40] Maya: yes; Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem options, KMS/HSM integration, and audit logs. Dedicated also supports customer-managed VPC peering and SAML. we'll attach SOC2/ISO docs.
[03:52] Marcus: ok. going back to cost model, what inputs do you need from us to produce accurate numbers?
[03:56] Daniel: sample prompt set (representative distribution), daily QPS profile (avg/peak), concurrency targets, desired latency SLOs, and whether you plan to use session caching aggressively. also any regulatory constraints that prevent hosted usage.
[04:08] Lena: we'll provide that. can you also propose a benchmark that tests tail latency under realistic traffic?
[04:13] Daniel: yes. propose a 2-week POC window: week 1 warm-up and functional validation, week 2 stress + benchmark. tests: 95/99 latency curves, throughput at target batch configs, cost per 1k tokens measured from telemetry, and quality check against baseline using 500 labeled prompts.
[04:28] Maya: timeline wise, if we get your artifacts by Mon 11/18 we can kick off a benchmark 11/20 and run two weeks, then meet 11/25 to review.
[04:36] Priya: can you run both hosted and dedicated benchmarks in parallel? we want apples-to-apples.
[04:39] Daniel: yes, we can run hosted at first then spin up a small dedicated pool for comparison. note dedicated requires a bit more lead time to provision GPU pool; for a short POC we can use a temporary reserved pool.
[04:52] Marcus: curious about quality regression risk when moving to quantized models — how do you evaluate that?
[04:56] Daniel: we run evals on your labeled prompts measuring ROUGE/EM/proxy metrics and human spot checks if needed. if quantization regresses over threshold we'll recommend a hybrid: host larger float models for critical flows and quantized for bulk.
[05:09] Lena: budget constraint: we're aiming for monthly inference spend under $25k in POC scale. can you model that?
[05:15] Maya: yes — we'll model spends for expected QPS and scale. if dedicated fixed costs push you over, we'll show break-even points and potential burst/auto-scaling policies to control spend.
[05:26] Marcus: what about caching strategies beyond KV? like response caching for idempotent queries?
[05:30] Daniel: yes, prefix cache for KV, response-level cache for exact-match responses, and client-side request coalescing. these reduce compute and cost but require invalidation strategies. response caching works well for support FAQ style flows.
[05:43] Priya: any gotchas on networking for Private? e.g., KMS access latency?
[05:47] Daniel: KMS egress can add tens of ms per key op; we recommend caching DEKs (data encryption keys) locally with HSM-backed rotation to avoid frequent KMS calls. we can document recommended key policies.
[05:58] Lena: ok, last bit — success criteria for POC. propose we define: (1) quality delta within 3% of baseline on labeled set, (2) 95th latency < 500ms for short paths and <1s for long paths, (3) total monthlyized cost projection under $25k at expected load, and (4) security checklist satisfied (SOC2 docs + KMS/VPC connectivity).
[06:20] Maya: that matches what we discussed. we'll codify those into the POC plan.
[06:24] Daniel: i'll include test scripts and telemetry dashboards we'll use.
[06:27] Maya: i'll send the pricing spreadsheet + next steps. any final questions?
[06:31] Marcus: one quick question — for your per-token numbers, do they include infra amortization and support overhead?
[06:36] Maya: hosted includes infra and normal support; dedicated shows amortized infra as the committed SKU and separately lists optional support/managed services. we'll make sure the spreadsheet has line items so you can toggle assumptions.
[06:47] Priya: sounds good.
[06:48] Lena: thanks everyone, looking forward to the benchmark.
[06:51] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts and a calendar invite for the kickoff.

--- End transcript ---
